Since the executable must remain \"cholesky\" with source cholesky.cpp and I can't add a new .cu file, I'll need to embed the CUDA compilation within that single source file.\n\nI can solve this in CMake by setting the LANGUAGE property on cholesky.cpp to CUDA so nvcc compiles it directly, letting it contain kernels and launch syntax. For the algorithm, I'm planning a blocked right-looking Cholesky decomposition on the GPU using custom shared-memory tiled kernels rather than cuBLAS, since that would introduce a new dependency — keeping the same row-major lower-triangular output semantics as the original, accepting minor floating-point rounding differences within the validation tolerance.\n\nDesigning the blocked algorithm: factor the small diagonal block sequentially in one GPU block, then solve the panel below it in parallel across rows using triangular substitution against the factored diagonal block.\n\nConfirming the upper triangle is never read during processing, only written at the end to zero — so our blocked version only needs to touch the lower triangle throughout and clear the rest at the finish.\n\nFor the positive-definite failure case, I need to preserve the original's behavior of reporting the first failing diagonal index. Since the diagonal block kernel processes sequentially, the smallest failing local index corresponds to the global index k0+local, so I can use a device flag checked after each block step via sync, accepting the modest per-step synchronization cost for correctness.\n\nBlock-based summation could introduce different rounding than sequential accumulation, which matters for the relative-error validation tolerance—especially for entries of A near zero, where even small absolute errors can blow up the relative error.\n\nThat risk is negligible and the same as in the original code, so I'll stick with double precision for correctness and plan a tiled GEMM kernel with 64x64 output tiles handled by 16x16 threads doing 4x4 outputs each, exploiting symmetry so only lower-triangular tiles need computing. I also expect the hash to differ slightly due to floating-point summation order, which is expected behavior.\n\nNow I'm thinking through the diagonal block factorization kernel design - weighing whether to use a single-threaded shared-memory approach versus parallelizing the inner-product reductions across threads, since the naive sequential version seems too slow for performance targets.\n\nI settle on a left-looking approach with NB threads per block: for each column j, one thread computes the diagonal pivot via a serial reduction with a fail check, then the remaining threads cooperatively update the column below it using the triangular solve formula.\n\nThe shared memory footprint for a 64x64 block of doubles stays around 32KB, and the per-block work is cheap enough that each panel should only take microseconds. I'm now double-checking that this left-looking scheme produces the same accumulation order as the original right-looking formulation, since the sum ordering needs to match for numerical equivalence.\n\nFor the panel-solve kernel, each row applies a forward substitution against the factored diagonal block: for row i and column j in the block, it computes (A[i][j] minus the running dot product with the lower-triangular factor) divided by the diagonal entry, with that dot product built up incrementally across the block's columns.\n\nI'm considering loading L11 into shared memory first since global reads for the diagonal block would otherwise be repeated across rows, then having a block of threads each own one row.
